intelligence.human_view: Think of the warehouse ledger saying a parcel shipped while the box is not on your porch. The ledger matters — it is how the warehouse runs — but telling the customer "the system says shipped" is not customer service. You walk out and look at the porch. The same law runs through the whole house: the speed on the car is the biggest numeral in front of you, the little dials off to the side; the road signs are one design, so you learn them once and read them at speed; the safety deposit box holds your real documents, not photocopies made from memory, and the bank genuinely cannot open it without you. And the builder who finishes your kitchen shows you the tap running, tells you honestly the back-order tile is not in yet, and stands there while you look it over and say what you think.
intelligence.simple_view: Imagine you rub out a drawing in your book. But a photo of it is still up on the class wall. Is it really gone? No, not for the children who walk past the wall. Taking the photo down is part of rubbing it out. Now look at a big score board at a game. The score is huge, so you can read it from far away. Think of a Lego castle on a magic shelf. Tomorrow you lift it down, still built, and keep building. That is the whole test. Look at the real thing, show your proof, and keep it safe.
intelligence.grandma_view: It is like the shop that chalked the day's prices on a board outside, love — if the price changed inside and nobody wiped the board, the board's price was the one you argued about at the till, because the board is what the street sees. Keep the board true, or don't chalk it. The bank statement that puts the balance big at the top lets you know where you stand in five seconds, and a good cookbook uses the same layout for every recipe, so you learn it once and cook anything in the book. And the tin box of important papers still does its job sixty years later because both halves were true from the start — real papers, and a real lock nobody else could open without asking.
intelligence.naya_view: Never report a state word as a serving verdict: verify deletions from feed bytes, diff the keys before touching stuck data, and record lag-window reads as TIMING with a re-check time. Fix the instrument in public, prove it both ways, count objects not substrings, retry a blocked call once as a gate, and route every proof artifact to its parent task. Assert hero order in review — number first, gauge second, ornament last — reuse the one canonical gauge, and reject per-board design invention; every number carries its explaining label. Close the current unit with its proof before opening the next, build hero lists from recorded pains, and capture the note at the moment of learning. Store harvested originals in the Box, enforce owner-scoped access at the data layer, and run the saved-game test — save, leave, return, retrieve the real thing — for every memory feature. Build new worlds as configurations of the universal app, never as new apps. Label every claim PROVEN or NOT PROVEN, prove mechanisms with repeated live trials, never swap a verified surface for an unverified newer one, and publish the eye's verdict verbatim. Prove the bridge landing by a live click, visual and text, and never open a second round on a file a round already owns.
